cards.claim: Fine-tuning at the target (higher) test resolution after training at lower resolution improves accuracy; this corrects the train-test resolution mismatch without requiring batch normalization fixes.
cards.conditions: EfficientNet models on ImageNet-2012; pre-trained models fine-tuned for a few epochs at target resolution; uses standard FixRes augmentation + label smoothing
cards.effect: Consistent accuracy improvements across all EfficientNet sizes (B0–L2): +0.5 to +1.7 pp on ImageNet without extra data (Tables 1–2), +0.3 to +0.5 pp with 300M unlabeled images (Table 1). Improvements persist on ImageNet-V2 cleaner test set (+1.5 to +2.3 pp; Table 5).
cards.evidence: Experimental results on ImageNet validation, ImageNet-V2, and ImageNet Real Labels; FixRes applied to publicly released pre-trained models
cards.quote: FixRes is a very simple fine-tuning that re-trains the classifier or a few top layers at the target resolution. Therefore, it has several advantages: 1. it is computationally cheap, the back-propagation is not performed on the whole network; 2. it works with any CNN classification architecture and is complementary with the other tricks mentioned above; 3. it can be applied on a CNN that comes from a possibly non reproducible source.

cards.claim: The train-test resolution mismatch (different region-of-classification sampling strategies at train vs. test) creates a data distribution skew that hurts model performance.
cards.conditions: Standard image classification practice: random crop + resize at training; center crop at test
cards.effect: Distribution mismatch; quantified indirectly by the gains from FixRes fine-tuning
cards.evidence: Problem statement validated by FixRes improvements across multiple architectures and datasets
cards.quote: While the crops extracted at training and test time have the same size, they arise from different RoCs, which skews the data distribution seen by the CNN.
